messages.author: 5a1b5a9591c118ef
messages.subject: Reduce + plyr combination
parts:
Hi list,

I was playing with a toy example,

library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(iris) +
geom_point(aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width))


all.plots <- dlply(iris, .(Species), function(d) p %+% d)

pdf("ply.pdf")
l_ply(all.plots, print)
dev.off()

which generates plots for different datasets. The anonymous function
feels a bit awkward, thus I tried to find an alternative. Reduce
immediately comes to mind,

all.plots2 <- Reduce("%+%", split(iris, iris$Species), p, accumulate=TRUE)

pdf("reduce.pdf")
l_ply(all.plots2[-1], print)
dev.off()


but now we've lost the nice splitting provided by plyr. Is there any
way to combine these two? Perhaps a new function for the plyr toolbox?
I imagine that other binary operators could use this trick (e.g. +
opts() ).

Cheers,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Reduce + plyr combination
parts:
Perhaps more relevant and useful, a **ply + Reduce combination could
be used to keep track of incremental changes to a ggplot, say, for
demonstration purposes,

p.bare = ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Petal.Length)) + geom_path()

params = list( aes(colour = Species),
facet_grid(.~Species),
list(geom_path(aes(y=Petal.Width), linetype=3), theme_bw())
)
p.incremental = Reduce(`+`, params, p.bare, acc = TRUE)

library(gridExtra)
do.call(grid.arrange, p.incremental)

Cheers,

Baptiste

messages.author: 5a1b5a9591c118ef
messages.subject: Re: Re: Reduce + plyr combination
parts:
Sure – sorry if it was less transparent than I thought. The idea comes
from the sort of incremental construct that I see many people use in
ggplot2,

p <- qplot(.. something basic ..)
p <- p + geom_path(.. or other ..)
p <- p + xlim(...)
p <- p + theme_bw()
p <- p + opts(legen.position="none")
...

Of course, you can also just add them all in one go, without
reassigning to p at each step. However, I figure the step-by-step
modification/assignment has its own attraction, namely you can
use/test intermediate plots. One obvious interest is when you want to
teach how ggplot2 works, showing visually the effect of each line.

The code I submitted earlier illustrates this idea, storing each step
as a plot of its own and comparing them visually on one page.

# this is the basic plot we want to modify
p.bare = ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Petal.Length)) + geom_path()

# this list contains incremental changes, to be applied one after the other

params = list( aes(colour = Species), # first, add a colour mapping
facet_grid(.~Species), # second, facetting
list(geom_path(aes(y=Petal.Width), linetype=3), theme_bw())
# third, add a layer, and also change the theme
)

# Reduce will execute the operation p[[ i+1 ]] <- p[[ i ]] + params [[ i+1 ]]
# and store the list of each intermediate p[[ i ]] (because accumulate = TRUE)
p.incremental = Reduce(`+`, params, p.bare, accumulate = TRUE)

# now we have a list of plots which we can compare visually
# using a grid.layout
library(gridExtra)
do.call(grid.arrange, p.incremental)

Does it make more sense?

Of course, now that I think about it I don't really see where plyr
would be needed.. Reduce seems to do the job just fine.

Cheers,

baptiste
